title: Correlation and Regression
outcomes: Describe bivariate data, a bivariate frequency table and its marginal and conditional distributions.

Identify positive, negative, linear and non-linear correlation from a scatter diagram and measure it with Karl Pearson's r, Spearman's rank correlation (with ties) and the coefficient of concurrent deviations.
Use the properties of r — limits, effect of change of origin and scale, coefficient of determination — and recognise spurious correlation.
Fit the regression lines of y on x and x on y by least squares, use them to estimate values and apply the properties of regression coefficients.

meta.exam_tip: Expect 5–6 MCQs: r from summary data, r = ±√(byx·bxy), byx = r σy/σx, regression lines meet at the means, which given line is y on x, rank correlation from Σd², concurrent deviations, change of origin/scale. Always check that byx × bxy ≤ 1.

concepts.title: Bivariate data and bivariate frequency distribution
body: When two variables are observed together on each unit — marks in two subjects, price and demand — the data are bivariate: pairs (xᵢ, yᵢ).
A bivariate (joint) frequency distribution, or two-way table, classifies the pairs by x-classes (columns) and y-classes (rows); each cell holds the frequency of that combination.

Marginal distributions: the row totals (distribution of y) and column totals (distribution of x). Conditional distribution: the distribution of one variable for a fixed class of the other (e.g. distribution of y for x in 40–50). Number of conditional distributions = number of classes of the conditioning variable.
concepts.analogy: A two-way table is a cricket scorecard by batsman and bowler; row totals give runs per batsman, column totals runs off each bowler.
concepts.work: A debtors ageing by region (two-way: age band × region) is a bivariate frequency table; management reads both the marginal totals and the conditional rows.

concepts.title: Types of correlation and the scatter diagram
body: Correlation: the two variables tend to move together. Positive — both move in the same direction (income and spending); negative — opposite directions (price and demand); zero — no linear relationship.
Linear correlation: the points lie close to a straight line; non-linear (curvilinear): they follow a curve.

Scatter diagram: plot each pair as a point. It shows direction, rough strength and whether the relation is linear or curvilinear, and it works for any type of relation — but it does not give a numerical measure. Always draw one first: r = 0 does not mean independence (y = x² over symmetric x gives r = 0).
concepts.analogy: A scatter diagram is a crowd photo from above — you see at once whether people are walking in a line, in a curve or milling about.
concepts.work: Analysts plot fuel cost against kilometres for a fleet before trusting a cost-per-km rate; outliers on the plot point to data errors or unusual trips.

concepts.title: Karl Pearson's product moment correlation coefficient
body: r = Cov(x, y)/(σx σy), where Cov(x, y) = Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ)/n. Working forms: r = Σuv/√(Σu² Σv²) with u = x − x̄, v = y − ȳ; or r = [nΣxy − ΣxΣy]/√{[nΣx² − (Σx)²][nΣy² − (Σy)²]}.

Properties: (i) r is a pure number (unit-free); (ii) −1 ≤ r ≤ 1 — r = 1 perfect positive, r = −1 perfect negative, r = 0 no linear correlation; (iii) r is unchanged by change of origin and scale — if u = (x − a)/b and v = (y − c)/d then r(u, v) = r(x, y) when b and d have the same sign, and r(u, v) = −r(x, y) when they have opposite signs; (iv) r = ±√(byx × bxy).
Change of origin (e.g. u = x − A) simplifies arithmetic without changing r.

concepts.analogy: r is a "togetherness score" from −1 (perfect mirror image) through 0 (strangers) to +1 (perfect twins).
concepts.work: Correlating monthly sales with advertising, or a stock's returns with the index (the basis of beta), is everyday analytical work.

concepts.title: Spearman's rank correlation and concurrent deviations
body: Spearman: rR = 1 − 6Σd²/[n(n² − 1)], d = difference between the two ranks of each item. Used for qualitative traits (beauty, honesty) or when only ranks are available. Lies between −1 and 1.
Ties: give tied items the average of the ranks they occupy; then rR = 1 − 6[Σd² + Σ(t³ − t)/12]/[n(n² − 1)], adding (t³ − t)/12 for every group of t tied values (in either series).

Coefficient of concurrent deviations: compare the direction of change of each series from one period to the next (+ or −); c = number of pairs with the same sign (concurrent), m = number of pairs of deviations (= n − 1). rC = ±√[±(2c − m)/m] — take the plus sign inside and outside when 2c − m > 0, the minus sign both places when 2c − m < 0. It too lies between −1 and 1; it shows direction quickly but is a rough measure.

concepts.analogy: Rank correlation asks only "did the two judges put the contestants in the same order?", not by how many points.
concepts.work: Comparing two credit-rating agencies' rankings of the same borrowers, or two interviewers' rankings of candidates, uses rank correlation.

concepts.title: Coefficient of determination and spurious correlation
body: Coefficient of determination = r² = explained variance ÷ total variance: the share of variation in y accounted for by x. r = 0.8 ⇒ r² = 0.64, i.e. 64% explained. Coefficient of non-determination = 1 − r² (unexplained share).

Spurious (nonsense) correlation: a correlation between variables with no causal link, produced by a third variable affecting both — e.g. rice output and iron output both rising with time. Remove the third variable's influence before interpreting r. Correlation never proves causation by itself.
concepts.analogy: Ice-cream sales and drowning cases rise together — not because ice-cream drowns people, but because summer drives both.
concepts.work: Before telling a client that a marketing campaign "caused" higher sales, check for seasonal effects or price changes that moved both.

concepts.title: Regression and the method of least squares
body: Regression estimates the average relationship between a dependent (explained) variable and an independent (explanatory) variable, so that one can be estimated from the other.

Regression line of y on x (to estimate y from x): y − ȳ = byx (x − x̄), with byx = Cov(x, y)/σx² = r σy/σx = Σuv/Σu². It minimises the sum of squared vertical deviations Σ(y − ŷ)² — the method of least squares. Normal equations for y = a + bx: Σy = na + bΣx and Σxy = aΣx + bΣx².
Regression line of x on y (to estimate x from y): x − x̄ = bxy (y − ȳ), bxy = r σx/σy = Σuv/Σv². It minimises horizontal squared deviations.
Use the y-on-x line to estimate y and the x-on-y line to estimate x — they are different lines unless r = ±1.
concepts.analogy: The least-squares line is the "fairest" straight line through a cloud of points — it keeps the total squared miss as small as possible.
concepts.work: Cost accountants split semi-variable costs into fixed and variable parts by regressing total cost on output (y = a + bx: a = fixed cost, b = variable cost per unit).

concepts.title: Properties of regression coefficients and lines
body: (i) Regression coefficients are unchanged by a shift of origin but change with scale: if u = (x − a)/p and v = (y − c)/q, then byx = (q/p) bvu and bxy = (p/q) buv.
(ii) The two lines intersect at (x̄, ȳ) — solve the two equations simultaneously to get the means.

(iii) r = ±√(byx × bxy), the geometric mean of the regression coefficients, taking their common sign. Hence both coefficients have the same sign as r, and byx × bxy = r² ≤ 1; they cannot both be numerically greater than 1.
(iv) The lines coincide (are identical) when r = ±1, and are perpendicular when r = 0.
Identifying lines from two equations: assume one is y on x, find byx and bxy; if their product is ≤ 1 (and signs agree) the assumption is right; otherwise swap.
concepts.analogy: Two regression lines are scissors hinged at the means: fully closed when r = ±1, opened to a right angle when r = 0.
concepts.work: When a client gives only two fitted equations, these properties let you recover the means and r in a minute — and spot an impossible pair of coefficients.

jobs.title: Separating fixed and variable cost by regression
jobs.role: Cost accountant in a manufacturing unit
jobs.situation: Monthly power cost and machine hours for 12 months are available. The plant head wants a budget formula.
steps: Plot cost (y) against machine hours (x) — check the relation is linear and remove months with breakdowns.
Fit y = a + bx by least squares: b = Σuv/Σu² (variable cost per hour), a = ȳ − b x̄ (fixed cost).
Report r²: if 0.9, about 90% of the cost variation is explained by machine hours.
Use the y-on-x line only within the range of hours observed — extrapolation is risky.
jobs.takeaway: Least-squares regression turns past cost data into a flexible-budget formula.

jobs.title: Testing an analytical review assumption
jobs.situation: You expect commission expense to move with sales. For 12 months r = 0.35, much lower than in prior years (0.9).
steps: A weak r means sales explain only about 12% (r²) of the variation in commission this year.
Scatter the data — one or two months may hold large one-off commissions or misposted entries.
Investigate those months with documents before concluding.
If the scheme changed (e.g. slab-based payouts), the relation may be non-linear — r understates it.
jobs.takeaway: A sudden fall in r is an audit signal: either the business changed or the books contain errors.

viva.q: State the important properties of the correlation coefficient.
viva.model: The correlation coefficient is a pure number without units. It always lies between minus one and plus one, both included. It is unaffected by a change of origin, and a change of scale does not change its value either, only its sign can change when the two scale factors have opposite signs. It is the geometric mean of the two regression coefficients.

viva.q: Explain Spearman's rank correlation coefficient. When is it preferred, and how are ties handled?
viva.model: Spearman's rank correlation is one minus six times the sum of squared rank differences, divided by n times n squared minus one. It is preferred for qualitative characteristics such as beauty or honesty that can only be ranked, or when the data are ranks. When values tie, each gets the average of the ranks they would have taken, and a correction of t cubed minus t over twelve is added to the sum of d squared for each tie.

viva.q: What is the difference between correlation and regression?
viva.model: Correlation measures the degree and direction of the linear relationship between two variables and is symmetric, so r of x and y equals r of y and x, and it is a pure number. Regression gives the average functional relationship, an equation used to estimate the value of a dependent variable from a known value of the independent variable. There are two regression lines, y on x and x on y, and regression coefficients have units.

viva.q: State the properties of regression coefficients and regression lines.
viva.model: The regression coefficients are unaffected by a change of origin but are affected by a change of scale. The two regression lines intersect at the point x bar, y bar, the means. The correlation coefficient is the geometric mean of the two regression coefficients, with the common sign, so both coefficients have the same sign and their product cannot exceed one. The lines coincide when r is plus or minus one and are perpendicular when r is zero.

viva.q: What is the coefficient of determination, and how is it interpreted?
viva.model: The coefficient of determination is the square of the correlation coefficient, r squared. It is the ratio of the explained variance to the total variance, so it shows the proportion of variation in the dependent variable explained by the independent variable. For example, if r is 0.8, r squared is 0.64, so 64 percent of the variation is explained. One minus r squared is the coefficient of non-determination, the unexplained part.

viva.q: What is spurious correlation? Give an example.
viva.model: Spurious or nonsense correlation is a correlation between two variables that have no cause and effect relationship; it appears because a third variable, such as time, influences both. For example, the production of rice and the production of iron may both rise over twenty years and show a high correlation, only because both grow with time. The influence of the third variable should be removed before reading meaning into r.

cases.title: Do training hours lift sales productivity?
cases.case: An FMCG company records, for 40 sales executives, the training hours attended last quarter (x) and the sales achieved this quarter in ₹ lakh (y). Summary: mean x = 12 hours, mean y = ₹40 lakh, SD of x = 2 hours, SD of y = ₹6 lakh, correlation coefficient r = 0.75. The HR head wants to predict sales for an executive who attends 14 hours.

mcqs.q: What is the regression coefficient of y on x?
mcqs.explain: b_yx = r × σy/σx = 0.75 × 6/2 = 2.25 (₹ lakh per extra training hour). 0.25 is b_xy.

mcqs.q: What sales would you predict for an executive with 14 training hours?
What proportion of the variation in sales is explained by training hours?
mcqs.explain: Coefficient of determination r² = 0.75² = 0.5625. The remaining 43.75% (1 − r²) is unexplained.

mcqs.q: Which conclusion is appropriate?
options: Training and sales are strongly positively related, but correlation alone does not prove that training causes higher sales
mcqs.explain: r = 0.75 shows a strong positive linear association; a third factor (e.g. motivated executives choose more training) could drive both — spurious correlation must be ruled out.
